scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: PANIC from the night shift -- an alert popped up and
now everyone thinks one of the big routers in the middle of the network, R6 or
maybe R7, has gone wrong overnight, but I don't know which one. Everything
crossing the middle is dying somewhere. Could someone look at R6 and R7 and
tell us it's fixed!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: The reported overnight alert about R6 or R7 causing widespread middle-network failures is not substantiated by any live evidence. A topology-wide reachability sweep shows pc0 to pc12 and the reverse path both completing with 0% packet loss. Phase A infrastructure sweep found zero ACL drops, no addressing anomalies, no duplicate MACs, and all host routes intact. Phase B OSPF snapshot confirms both accused routers are fully operational: r6 holds three Full OSPF adjacencies in area 0.0.0.1 (with r4, r5, and r7) and carries 55 OSPF routes; r7 holds one Full adjacency with r6 (its only physical peer) and carries 57 OSPF routes. The TC snapshot shows clean pfifo_fast qdiscs with no shaping or corruption. Phase D pressure sweep found no stressed or resource-exhausted devices. Two longstanding anomalies appear in the snapshot — r8 has an orphaned OSPF area 0.0.0.2 with no peers, and r13 has its ospfd daemon absent — but both are chronic pre-existing conditions documented across multiple prior diagnostic sessions of this lab topology, neither lies on the pc0–pc12 forwarding path, and neither affects any observable traffic. The alarm was either a transient false positive that self-cleared, or was triggered by one of these pre-existing configuration artifacts rather than an acute failure. No corrective action is required for r6 or r7.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly confirms R6/R7 are operational with a Full R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency and reports PC0↔PC12 reachability with 0% loss, matching the baseline-healthy expectation.

The agent's investigation ran appropriate probes (reachability, infra, OSPF, TC, pressure) and the conclusions mostly follow from observed results. A few specific claims in the final writeup (e.g., "no duplicate MACs" and exact OSPF route counts) are not clearly supported by the visible logs, so grounding is slightly weakened though causality and overall coverage are strong.
